::: {.question-card}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/21 & 9231/22 · Question 8 · 14 marks

**(a)** Find the values of $a$ for which the system of equations

$$
3x+y+z=0,\qquad ax+6y-z=0,\qquad ay-2z=0
$$

does not have a unique solution. **[3]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&1\\0&6&-1\\0&0&-2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to find the inverse of $A^2$. **[4]**

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A^5=PDP^{-1}$. **[7]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The system fails to have a unique solution exactly when $\det M=0$:

$$
\begin{vmatrix}3&1&1\\a&6&-1\\0&a&-2\end{vmatrix}
=3(-12+a)-(-2a)+a^2
=a^2+5a-36=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{a=4\ \text{or}\ a=-9}.
$$

**(b)** The eigenvalues of $A$ are $3$, $6$, $-2$, so the characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-3)(\lambda-6)(\lambda+2)=\lambda^3-7\lambda^2+36=0.
$$

Thus $A^3-7A^2+36I=0$, and multiplying through by $(A^{-1})^2$ gives

$$
36(A^{-1})^2=7I-A.
$$

Computing $(A^{-1})^2$ from this,

$$
\boxed{(A^{-1})^2=\frac1{36}
\begin{pmatrix}4&-1&-1\\0&1&1\\0&0&9\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** With eigenvalues $3,6,-2$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\3\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}-9\\5\\40\end{pmatrix},
$$

taking them as columns,

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&-9\\0&3&5\\0&0&40\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
D=\begin{pmatrix}3^5&0&0\\0&6^5&0\\0&0&(-2)^5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}243&0&0\\0&7776&0\\0&0&-32\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus $\boxed{A^5=PDP^{-1}}$.

</details>

<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/21/M/J/2020, Q8; 9231/22/M/J/2020, Q8.</div>

### 2020 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 3 · 8 marks

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}5&-1&7\\0&6&0\\7&7&5\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Find the eigenvalues of $A$. **[4]**

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to find $A^{-1}$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}5-\lambda&-1&7\\0&6-\lambda&0\\7&7&5-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0,
$$

which expands to

$$
-\lambda^3+16\lambda^2-36\lambda-144=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(\lambda+2)(\lambda-6)(\lambda-12)=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\lambda=-2,\ 6,\ 12}.
$$

**(b)** The characteristic equation gives

$$
-A^3+16A^2-36A-144I=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
144A^{-1}=-A^2+16A-36I.
$$

Computing

$$
A^2=\begin{pmatrix}74&38&70\\0&36&0\\70&70&74\end{pmatrix},
$$

gives

$$
\boxed{A^{-1}=\frac1{24}
\begin{pmatrix}-5&-9&7\\0&4&0\\7&7&-5\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-p2-2020-mj-23-q3"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2020, Q3.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/21 & 9231/23 · Question 7 · 9 marks

The matrix $P$ is given by

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&4&2\\0&-1&1\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** State the eigenvalues of $P$. **[1]**

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $P$ to find $P^{-1}$. **[4]**

The $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has distinct eigenvalues $b$, $-1$, $1$ with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Find $A$ in terms of $b$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** For an upper triangular matrix the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries:

$$
\boxed{1,\ -1,\ 2}.
$$

**(b)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-1)(\lambda+1)(\lambda-2)=\lambda^3-2\lambda^2-\lambda+2=0,
$$

so $P^3-2P^2-P+2I=0$. Multiplying through by $P^{-1}$,

$$
2P^{-1}=I+2P-P^2.
$$

Computing

$$
P^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&10\\0&1&1\\0&0&4\end{pmatrix},
$$

gives

$$
\boxed{P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&4&-3\\0&-1&\frac12\\0&0&\frac12\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** Using $A=PDP^{-1}$ with

$$
D=\begin{pmatrix}b&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&4&2\\0&-1&1\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix},
$$

the eigenvectors are the columns of $P$ in the same order as the eigenvalues in $D$. Hence

$$
\boxed{A=\begin{pmatrix}b&4b+4&-3b-1\\0&-1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-p2-2020-on-21-23-q7"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/21/O/N/2020, Q7; 9231/23/O/N/2020, Q7.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 9 · 15 marks

It is given that $a$ is a positive constant.

**(a)** Show that the system of equations

$$
ax+(2a+5)y+(a+1)z=1,\qquad -4y=2,\qquad 3y-z=3
$$

has a unique solution, and interpret this situation geometrically. **[3]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}a&2a+5&a+1\\0&-4&0\\0&3&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Show that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $a$, $-1$ and $-4$. **[2]**

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=P\begin{pmatrix}a&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&-4\end{pmatrix}P^{-1}.
$$

**[5]**

**(d)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to find $A^{-1}$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a&2a+5&a+1\\0&-4&0\\0&3&-1\end{vmatrix}=4a\ne0
$$

since $a>0$. Therefore the system has a unique solution: the three planes intersect at a single point.

**(b)** The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}a-\lambda&2a+5&a+1\\0&-4-\lambda&0\\0&3&-1-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0,
$$

giving

$$
(a-\lambda)(-4-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{\lambda=a,\ -1,\ -4}.
$$

**(c)** Corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
\lambda=a:\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\lambda=-1:\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\lambda=-4:\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&0&-1\\0&-1&1\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-a)(\lambda+1)(\lambda+4)
=\lambda^3+(5-a)\lambda^2+(4-5a)\lambda-4a=0.
$$

So

$$
A^3+(5-a)A^2+(4-5a)A-4aI=0,
$$

and multiplying through by $A^{-1}$,

$$
4aA^{-1}=A^2+(5-a)A+(4-5a)I.
$$

Computing $A^2$ and substituting gives

$$
\boxed{A^{-1}=\frac1{4a}
\begin{pmatrix}4&5a+8&4a+4\\0&-a&0\\0&-3a&-4a\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-p2-2020-on-22-q9"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2020, Q9.</div>
:::

### 2021

::: {.question-card}
### 2021 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 8 · 13 marks

**(a)** Find the value of $a$ for which the system of equations

$$
13x+18y-28z=0,\qquad -4x-ay+8z=0,\qquad 2x+6y-5z=0
$$

does not have a unique solution. **[2]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}13&18&-28\\-4&-1&8\\2&6&-5\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Find the eigenvalue of $A$ corresponding to the eigenvector $\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}$. **[1]**

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A=PDP^{-1}$. **[8]**

**(d)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to find $A^{-1}$ in terms of $A$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The system fails to have a unique solution when

$$
\det\begin{pmatrix}13&18&-28\\-4&-a&8\\2&6&-5\end{pmatrix}
=8-\frac{9a}{4}=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{a=\frac{32}9}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
A\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}13&18&-28\\-4&-1&8\\2&6&-5\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}
=-\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\lambda=-1}.
$$

**(c)** The characteristic equation is

$$
\det(A-\lambda I)=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
-\lambda^3+7\lambda^2-7\lambda-15=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(\lambda+1)(\lambda-3)(\lambda-5)=0.
$$

So $\lambda=-1,\ 3,\ 5$ with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}2&1&-1\\0&1&2\\1&1&1\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&3&0\\0&0&5\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** Since $A$ satisfies its characteristic equation,

$$
A^3-7A^2+7A+15I=0.
$$

Multiplying through by $A^{-1}$,

$$
A^2-7A+7I+15A^{-1}=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{A^{-1}=\frac1{15}\left(-A^2+7A-7I\right)}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-p2-2021-mj-23-q8"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2021, Q8.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 6 · 11 marks

The matrix $P$ is given by

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&6&6\\0&2&6\\0&0&-3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Use the characteristic equation of $P$ to find $P^{-1}$. **[5]**

**(b)** Find the matrix $A$ such that

$$
P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&5&0\\0&0&6\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**[4]**

**(c)** State the eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of $A^3$. **[2]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda+3)=\lambda^3-7\lambda+6=0.
$$

So $P^3-7P+6I=0$, and multiplying through by $P^{-1}$ gives

$$
P^2-7I+6P^{-1}=0.
$$

Computing

$$
P^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&18&24\\0&4&6\\0&0&9\end{pmatrix},
$$

gives

$$
\boxed{P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&-3&-4\\0&\frac12&1\\0&0&-\frac13\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(b)** $P^{-1}AP=D$ gives $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $D=\operatorname{diag}(4,5,6)$:

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&6&6\\0&2&6\\0&0&-3\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}4&0&0\\0&5&0\\0&0&6\end{pmatrix}
P^{-1}
=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}4&3&2\\0&5&-2\\0&0&6\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** The eigenvalues of $A^3$ are

$$
\boxed{64,\ 125,\ 216},
$$

with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}6\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\\-3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2022

### 2022 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 3 · 7 marks

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}6&-9&5\\5&-8&5\\1&-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Find the eigenvalues of $A$. **[4]**

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to show that

$$
A^{-1}=pA^2+qI,
$$

where $p$ and $q$ are constants to be determined. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}6-\lambda&-9&5\\5&-8-\lambda&5\\1&-1&2-\lambda\end{vmatrix}=0,
$$

which expands to

$$
\lambda^3-7\lambda+6=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda+3)=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\lambda=1,\ 2,\ -3}.
$$

**(b)** Since $A$ satisfies its own characteristic equation,

$$
A^3-7A+6I=0.
$$

Multiplying through by $A^{-1}$,

$$
A^2-7I+6A^{-1}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{A^{-1}=-\frac16A^2+\frac76I}.
$$

So $p=-\dfrac16$ and $q=\dfrac76$.

</details>

### 2023

### 2023 May/June · 9231/21 · Question 1 · 5 marks

**(a)** Show that the system of equations

$$
x+2y+3z=1,\qquad 4x+5y+6z=1,\qquad 7x+8y+9z=1
$$

does not have a unique solution. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that the system of equations in part (a) is consistent. Interpret this situation geometrically. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}1&2&3\\4&5&6\\7&8&9\end{vmatrix}
=(45-48)-2(36-42)+3(32-35)=-3+12-9=0.
$$

Since the determinant is zero, the system does not have a unique solution.

**(b)** Using row operations (or eliminating variables), the three equations reduce to a single consistent relation, for example

$$
z=\frac13(1-x-2y),\qquad y=-2x-1.
$$

The system is therefore consistent, with infinitely many solutions. Geometrically, the three planes form a sheaf: they intersect along a common line.

</details>

### 2023 May/June · 9231/21 · Question 5 · 10 marks

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}18&5&-11\\8&6&-4\\32&10&-20\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Show that the characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
m^3-4m^2-20m+48=0
$$

and hence find the eigenvalues of $A$. **[4]**

**(b)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A^5=PDP^{-1}$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Expanding $\det(A-mI)=0$ gives

$$
m^3-4m^2-20m+48=0,
$$

which factorises as

$$
(m-2)(m+4)(m-6)=0.
$$

So

$$
\boxed{m=2,\ -4,\ 6}.
$$

**(b)** Corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
m=2:\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
m=-4:\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
m=6:\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\\2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\-1&0&2\\1&2&2\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}2^5&0&0\\0&(-4)^5&0\\0&0&6^5\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}32&0&0\\0&-1024&0\\0&0&7776\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/21/M/J/2023, Q5.</div>

### 2023 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 6 · 10 marks

The matrix $P$ is given by

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&1\\0&2&1\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** State the eigenvalues of $P$. **[1]**

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $P$ to find $P^{-1}$. **[4]**

The $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has distinct non-zero eigenvalues $a$, $1$, $2$ with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}-1\\2\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Find $A^{-1}$ in terms of $a$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** For an upper triangular matrix,

$$
\boxed{1,\ 2,\ -1}.
$$

**(b)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda+1)=\lambda^3-2\lambda^2-\lambda+2=0,
$$

so $P^3-2P^2-P+2I=0$. Multiplying through by $P^{-1}$,

$$
2P^{-1}=I+2P-P^2.
$$

Computing

$$
P^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&-3&-1\\0&4&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix},
$$

gives

$$
\boxed{P^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac12&\frac32\\0&\frac12&\frac12\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** With eigenvectors as the columns of $P$ and eigenvalues $a,1,2$,

$$
A^{-1}=P
\begin{pmatrix}\frac1a&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&\frac12\end{pmatrix}
P^{-1}
=\boxed{\frac12\begin{pmatrix}\frac2a&-1&1\\0&2&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2024

::: {.question-card}
### 2024 May/June · 9231/21 & 9231/22 · Question 8 · 16 marks

**(a)** Find the set of values of $a$ for which the system of equations

$$
6x+ay=3,\qquad 2x-y=1,\qquad x+5y+4z=2
$$

has a unique solution. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that the system of equations in part (a) is consistent for all values of $a$. **[3]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}6&0&0\\2&-1&0\\1&5&4\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that

$$
(14A+24I)^2=PDP^{-1}.
$$

**[7]**

**(d)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to show that

$$
(14A+24I)^2=A^4(A+bI)^2,
$$

where $b$ is an integer to be determined. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The system has a unique solution when the determinant is non-zero:

$$
\begin{vmatrix}6&a&0\\2&-1&0\\1&5&4\end{vmatrix}
=4(-6-2a)=-8a-24.
$$

So the unique-solution set is

$$
\boxed{a\ne-3}.
$$

**(b)** If $a\ne-3$ the system has a unique solution, so it is consistent. If $a=-3$, the equations reduce to

$$
6x-3y=3,\qquad 2x-y=1,\qquad x+5y+4z=2,
$$

which are consistent (e.g. $(1,0,\frac14)$ is a solution). Hence the system is consistent for all $a$.

**(c)** The eigenvalues of $A$ are $6$, $-1$, $4$, with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}14\\4\\17\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}14&0&0\\4&-1&0\\17&1&1\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}(14\cdot6+24)^2&0&0\\0&(-14+24)^2&0\\0&0&(56+24)^2\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}11664&0&0\\0&100&0\\0&0&6400\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-6)(\lambda+1)(\lambda-4)=\lambda^3-9\lambda^2+14\lambda+24=0,
$$

so

$$
14A+24I=-A^3+9A^2=A^2(9I-A).
$$

Squaring,

$$
(14A+24I)^2=A^4(9I-A)^2=A^4(A-9I)^2.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{b=-9}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="matrices-p2-2024-mj-21-22-q8"> Completed</label>

### 2024 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 8 · 14 marks

The planes $P_1$ and $P_2$ do not intersect and are both perpendicular to $\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$. The line $l$ intersects $P_1$ at the point $(1,6,0)$ and intersects $P_2$ at the point $(3,-6,0)$.

**(a)** Find Cartesian equations of $P_1$ and $P_2$. **[3]**

**(b)** Express the vector equation of $l$ in the form $\mathbf r=\mathbf a+\lambda\mathbf b$, where $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are vectors to be determined, and hence show that for points on $l$,

$$
\frac12x+\frac1{12}y=1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad z=0.
$$

**[2]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\1&2&3\\\frac12&\frac1{12}&0\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Show that the characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
-\lambda^3+3\lambda^2+\frac74\lambda=0
$$

and hence find the eigenvalues of $A$. **[3]**

**(d)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A^n=PDP^{-1}$, where $n$ is a positive integer. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since both planes are perpendicular to $\mathbf i+2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$, their equations are $x+2y+3z=d$. Substituting the two given points,

$$
\boxed{P_1:x+2y+3z=13},\qquad
\boxed{P_2:x+2y+3z=-9}.
$$

**(b)** The direction of $l$ is

$$
\begin{pmatrix}3\\-6\\0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-12\\0\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\\0\end{pmatrix}
+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}2\\-12\\0\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

Thus $z=0$, and

$$
x=1+2\lambda,\qquad y=6-12\lambda.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac12x+\frac1{12}y
=\frac12(1+2\lambda)+\frac1{12}(6-12\lambda)
=\frac12+\lambda+\frac12-\lambda
=1.
$$

**(c)** Expanding $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$,

$$
(1-\lambda)\left(-\lambda(2-\lambda)-\frac14\right)-2\left(-\lambda-\frac32\right)+3\left(\frac1{12}-\frac12(2-\lambda)\right)=0,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
-\lambda^3+3\lambda^2+\frac74\lambda=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\lambda\left(\lambda^2-3\lambda-\frac74\right)=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\lambda=0,\ \frac72,\ -\frac12}.
$$

**(d)** Corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
\lambda=0:\begin{pmatrix}3\\-18\\11\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\lambda=\frac72:\begin{pmatrix}6\\6\\1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\lambda=-\frac12:\begin{pmatrix}-6\\-6\\7\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}3&6&-6\\-18&6&-6\\11&1&7\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&(\frac72)^n&0\\0&0&(-\frac12)^n\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2024 October/November · 9231/21 & 9231/23 · Question 4 · 9 marks

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}-11&1&8\\0&-2&0\\-16&1&13\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Show that $\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and state the corresponding eigenvalue. **[2]**

**(b)** Show that the characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
m^3-19m-30=0
$$

and hence find the other eigenvalues of $A$. **[3]**

**(c)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to find $A^{-1}$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$
A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-11+1+8\\-2\\-16+1+13\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-2\\-2\end{pmatrix}
=-2\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

So the corresponding eigenvalue is

$$
\boxed{\lambda=-2}.
$$

**(b)** Expanding $\det(A-mI)=0$,

$$
(-11-m)(-2-m)(13-m)+128(-2-m)=0,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
m^3-19m-30=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(m+2)(m-5)(m+3)=0.
$$

The other eigenvalues are

$$
\boxed{m=5\ \text{and}\ m=-3}.
$$

**(c)** Since $A$ satisfies $A^3-19A-30I=0$,

$$
30A^{-1}=A^2-19I.
$$

Computing

$$
A^2=\begin{pmatrix}-7&-5&16\\0&4&0\\-32&-5&41\end{pmatrix},
$$

gives

$$
\boxed{A^{-1}=\frac1{30}
\begin{pmatrix}-26&-5&16\\0&-15&0\\-32&-5&22\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2024 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 8 · 14 marks

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}-2&0&0\\0&7&9\\4&1&7\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** Show that the characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
m^3-12m^2+12m+80=0
$$

and find the eigenvalues of $A$. **[4]**

**(b)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to show that

$$
A^4=pA^2+qA+rI,
$$

where $p$, $q$ and $r$ are integers to be determined. **[4]**

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $(A-3I)^4=PDP^{-1}$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Expanding $\det(A-mI)=0$,

$$
(-2-m)\bigl((7-m)^2-9\bigr)=0,
$$

so

$$
m^3-12m^2+12m+80=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
(m+2)(m-4)(m-10)=0.
$$

The eigenvalues are

$$
\boxed{m=-2,\ 4,\ 10}.
$$

**(b)** Since $A^3-12A^2+12A+80I=0$,

$$
A^4-12A^3+12A^2+80A=0.
$$

Substituting $A^3=12A^2-12A-80I$,

$$
A^4=12(12A^2-12A-80I)-12A^2-80A
=\boxed{132A^2-224A-960I}.
$$

So $p=132$, $q=-224$, $r=-960$.

**(c)** Corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
m=-2:\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
m=4:\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
m=10:\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&0\\1&3&3\\-1&-1&1\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}(-5)^4&0&0\\0&1^4&0\\0&0&7^4\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}625&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&2401\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

:::

### 2025 May/June · 9231/21 & 9231/22 · Question 8 · 13 marks

**(a)** It is given that $m$ is an eigenvalue of the non-singular square matrix $A$, with corresponding eigenvector $\mathbf e$. Show that $\mathbf e$ is an eigenvector of $A^3$ with corresponding eigenvalue $m^3$. **[2]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}-1&3&4\\0&1&0\\0&-2&5\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(b)** Show that the eigenvalues of $A$ are $-1$, $1$ and $5$. **[2]**

**(c)** Find a matrix $P$ and a diagonal matrix $D$ such that $A-2I=PDP^{-1}$. **[6]**

**(d)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to show that

$$
(A-2I)^3=aA^2+bA+cI,
$$

where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants to be determined. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since $A\mathbf e=m\mathbf e$,

$$
A^3\mathbf e=A^2(A\mathbf e)=A^2(m\mathbf e)=mA(A\mathbf e)=m^2A\mathbf e=m^3\mathbf e.
$$

So $\mathbf e$ is an eigenvector of $A^3$ with eigenvalue $m^3$.

**(b)** The characteristic equation is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}-1-\lambda&3&4\\0&1-\lambda&0\\0&-2&5-\lambda\end{vmatrix}
=(-1-\lambda)(1-\lambda)(5-\lambda)=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\lambda=-1,\ 1,\ 5}.
$$

**(c)** Corresponding eigenvectors are

$$
\lambda=-1:\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\lambda=1:\begin{pmatrix}5\\2\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\lambda=5:\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Thus

$$
\boxed{P=\begin{pmatrix}1&5&2\\0&2&0\\0&1&3\end{pmatrix}},
\qquad
\boxed{D=\begin{pmatrix}-3&0&0\\0&-1&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(d)** The characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
(\lambda+1)(\lambda-1)(\lambda-5)=\lambda^3-5\lambda^2-\lambda+5=0,
$$

so

$$
A^3=5A^2+A-5I.
$$

Expanding $(A-2I)^3=A^3-6A^2+12A-8I$ and substituting,

$$
(A-2I)^3=-A^2+13A-13I.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{a=-1,\ b=13,\ c=-13}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/21 & 9231/23 · Question 6 · 10 marks

The matrix $P$ has non-zero eigenvalues and is given by

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}a&1&1\\0&2a&-1\\0&0&-3a\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(a)** State, in terms of $a$, the eigenvalues of $P$. **[1]**

**(b)** **(i)** Find $P^2$ in terms of $a$. **[1]**

**(ii)** Use the characteristic equation of $P$ to find $P^{-1}$ in terms of $a$. **[3]**

The $3\times3$ matrix $A$ has eigenvalues $1$, $2$, $3$ with corresponding eigenvectors

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a\\0\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\2a\\0\end{pmatrix},\quad
\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\-3a\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(c)** Find $A$ in terms of $a$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** For an upper triangular matrix,

$$
\boxed{a,\ 2a,\ -3a}.
$$

**(b)(i)**

$$
\boxed{P^2=\begin{pmatrix}a^2&3a&-2a-1\\0&4a^2&a\\0&0&9a^2\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(ii)** The characteristic equation is

$$
(\lambda-a)(\lambda-2a)(\lambda+3a)=\lambda^3-7a^2\lambda+6a^3=0,
$$

so $P^3-7a^2P+6a^3I=0$. Multiplying through by $P^{-1}$,

$$
6a^3P^{-1}=7a^2I-P^2.
$$

Using part (b)(i),

$$
\boxed{P^{-1}=\frac1{6a^3}
\begin{pmatrix}6a^2&-3a&2a+1\\0&3a^2&-a\\0&0&-2a^2\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

**(c)** With the eigenvectors as columns,

$$
P=\begin{pmatrix}a&1&1\\0&2a&-1\\0&0&-3a\end{pmatrix},
$$

so

$$
A=P\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}P^{-1}
=\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}1&\frac1{2a}&\frac{1-4a}{6a^2}\\0&2&\frac1{3a}\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 8 · 15 marks

**(a)** Find the values of $k$ for which the system of equations

$$
x-y+2kz=1,\qquad kx+y+2z=2,\qquad 2x-y+z=3
$$

does not have a unique solution. **[3]**

**(b)** Given that $k=-\frac12$, show that the system of equations in part (a) is inconsistent. Interpret this situation geometrically. **[3]**

**(c)** Given instead that $k=-1$, show that the system of equations in part (a) is also inconsistent. Interpret this situation geometrically. **[4]**

The matrix $A$ is given by

$$
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&-2\\-1&1&2\\2&-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**(d)** Use the characteristic equation of $A$ to show that

$$
A^4=pA^2+qA
$$

where $p$ and $q$ are integers to be determined. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}1&-1&2k\\k&1&2\\2&-1&1\end{vmatrix}=2k^2+3k+1=0.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{k=-1\ \text{or}\ k=-\frac12}.
$$

**(b)** When $k=-\frac12$, the equations become

$$
x-y-z=1,\qquad -\frac12x+y+2z=2,\qquad 2x-y+z=3.
$$

Adding the first two equations gives $\frac12x+z=3$, while the third equation gives $2x-y+z=3$; eliminating variables leads to the contradiction $1=-2$. Therefore the system is inconsistent. Geometrically, the planes form a triangular prism (no common point).

**(c)** When $k=-1$, the equations become

$$
x-y-2z=1,\qquad -x+y+2z=2,\qquad 2x-y+z=3.
$$

The first two equations give $1=-2$, a contradiction. So the system is inconsistent. Geometrically, two planes are parallel (and not identical), with the third plane not parallel to them.

**(d)** The characteristic equation of $A$ is

$$
\begin{vmatrix}1-\lambda&-1&-2\\-1&1-\lambda&2\\2&-1&1-\lambda\end{vmatrix}
=-\lambda^3+3\lambda^2-8\lambda=0.
$$

So $A^3=3A^2-8A$. Multiplying by $A$,

$$
A^4=3A^3-8A^2=3(3A^2-8A)-8A^2=A^2-24A.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{p=1,\ q=-24}.
$$

</details>
